BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: An upper level ridge will remain overhead on Tuesday with continued dry and slightly warmer temperatures. Winds will become breezy ahead of a low that will weaken and move through on Wednesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Isolated to scattered showers through this afternoon.
- Widespread rain and high elevation snow tonight into Sunday. A slight chance of thunderstorms late this afternoon through this evening.
- Cooler with gusty winds Sunday, and especially Sunday night, then drying and warming Monday through Wednesday. Slight chance of precipitation late week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: An upper low off the Oregon coast will slowly move inland tonight into Sunday. The track of the low and southerly flow will transport subtropical moisture over the Desert Southwest northward into our area. Shower activity will initially be isolated to scattered through the afternoon, then increase this evening and become widespread overnight as the low advances and moisture increases. A 10-20% chance of thunderstorms will develop across southern Idaho and far southeast Oregon late this afternoon through tonight with lower chances elsewhere. Brief heavy rain is possible from thunderstorms. Precipitation will continue into Sunday as moisture wraps around the low, decreasing from west to east. Showers will finally come to an end Sunday evening across south-central Idaho.

Precipitation amounts from this system will be substantial, with 0.25 to 0.50 inch likely across most of southwest Idaho and far southeast Oregon. However, there is a 10-20% chance of heavy rainfall totals in excess of 1 inch in the lower elevations of southwest Idaho. Lower amounts are expected to the west including Burns and Baker City Oregon. Totals of 0.50 to 1 inch are expected in the Boise mountains and southwest Idaho highlands, with locally higher amounts possible. Snow levels will be 6500-8000 feet today, then lower to 5500-7000 feet Sunday morning behind a cold front, lowest across southeast Oregon. This will limit significant snow accumulation to elevations above 7000-8000 feet with several inches of snow, and a dusting possible down to 6000 feet.

Temperatures today will be near normal with valley highs in the mid to upper 50s, with most areas cooling 5 to 10 degrees on Sunday behind the cold front. Winds will be breezy on Sunday with gusts 20 to 35 mph, except up to 45 mph east of Boise through the Magic Valley, strongest Sunday night. Winds will taper off on Monday as the low moves east and an upper level ridge moves overhead. This will bring dry conditions and warming temperatures at higher elevations while lower elevations see similar temperatures as a weak inversion develops.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: An upper level ridge will remain overhead on Tuesday with continued dry and slightly warmer temperatures. Winds will become breezy ahead of a low that will weaken and move through on Wednesday. Additional troughs are expected late week, increasing precipitation chances to 10-30% late Wednesday and Thursday, and further rising to 20-50% on Friday. These systems will be weak, keeping similar, near-normal temperatures from day to day. A ridge of high pressure is likely to build overhead on Saturday with a return to dry conditions.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: On Tue, an upper level ridge will begin to build into the area with dry conditions and near seasonal temperatures. Looking ahead to the middle part of next week, there is considerable uncertainty as to whether another system will affect the area or not.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of fog again late tonight through Sunday morning across portions of northeast and eastern Colorado.
- Unsettled weather returns late Sunday and Monday.Mountain snow is likely (>70% chance) above 8500ft during thistime. High uncertainty remains for the foothills and plains.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Once again will be dealing with areas of dense later tonight thru Sat morning over portions of the plains and I-25 Corridor. Timing of its development, closer to nrn areas of the I-25 Corridor and over Weld county, is still a bit uncertain. However, believe it will begin developing around 09z and then spread south into the Denver Metro by 11z or so. Fog will likely last thru 16z and then gradually lift in most areas.

Meanwhile, for the rest of Sat, a disturbance embedded in SW flow aloft will move across the higher terrain by midday. This feature will bring a chc of showers to portions of the higher terrain as it moves across. Over the plains, expect mainly dry conditions with highs in the mid 50's to lower 60's.

Looking ahead to Sun, the ECMWF and GFS have an elongated upper level trough moving into the nrn Rockies and Great Basin by late Sun aftn. Ahead of this feature, rather stg SSW flow aloft will be over the area with an influx of subtropical moisture. For most of the day, the best chc of precip will stay to the west but by late aftn should see an increasing chc of showers over the higher terrain. Across the plains, sfc low pres will extend from ern WY into ern CO with gusty southerly winds by aftn.

For Sun night into Mon, the elongated upper level trough will move eastward with a couple pieces of energy associated with it. One piece of energy will move into the Dakota's while the 2nd piece of energy tracks across srn CO/nrn NM. As the main upper level trough and associated QG ascent moves across will see rain and snow over the higher terrain Sun night into Mon. Over nern CO, a cold front will move across Mon morning with gusty NNW winds behind it. QG fields still show favorable mid level ascent across the plains thru the aftn so will keep in a good chc of showers over the plains. However, the downslope NNW winds may reduce precip chances closer to the I-25 Corridor.

By Mon night, the main upper level trough will move east of the area with drier air moving in behind the system. Will continue to see a good chc of showers Mon evening mainly over the east central plains. However, by late Mon evening should see precip gradually end.

On Tue, an upper level ridge will begin to build into the area with dry conditions and near seasonal temperatures. Looking ahead to the middle part of next week, there is considerable uncertainty as to whether another system will affect the area or not. The latest GFS tracks this system across the nrn Rockies while the ECMWF has it moving across Colorado.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: A much drier airmass will rotate into the area after midnight Monday night, bringing an abrupt end to precipitation from north to south. Gusty northwest winds will continue into Tuesday, but temperatures should rebound to near seasonal averages.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Intermittent, locally dense fog Saturday morning will clear out by midday. Another round of fog is possible Saturday night into Sunday morning.
- Mild conditions are expected for Halloween (Saturday), though a few showers will be possible along and west of I-25.
- A complex but disorganized storm system will move into the area Sunday, bringing cooler temperatures and a chance for rain and high elevation snow showers.
- A second round of precipitation is increasingly likely to develop over portions of the High Plains Monday into Monday evening.
- Widespread blustery conditions are anticipated Monday into Tuesday along and east of the Laramie range.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Spooky fog has settled in over portions of the High Plains to start this Halloween. This morning's fog is a bit more intermittent than yesterday, but at least patchy fog encompasses much of the High Plains. Expect fog to roll in and out a few times this morning. Dense Fog Advisories have been posted for much of the I-25 corridor and portions of the I-80 corridor, but may need to be expanded if fog pushes into the central/northern panhandle as well. Cloud cover and abundant low-level moisture are supporting very mild temperatures for this time of year, with today expected to start off in the upper 30s to mid 40s for all areas. The vort-max moving into the area out of the southwest is a bit ahead of schedule, as mid to upper level moisture is already pushing into southern Wyoming as indicated by GOES water vapor imagery. Expect shower activity to kick up over the next several hours, mainly in Carbon county, but rainfall amounts will be minimal. We actually have a fairly dry airmass in place west of the Laramie range, but expect dewpoints to rise as light rain falls into the dry boundary later. The shortwave trough axis should push through around midday, decreasing coverage of shower activity afterwards, though some shallow instability should keep isolated showers going along and west of the Laramie range through the early evening hours.

This year's trick-or-treat forecast is unusually mild. Sunset temperatures will be generally in the 50s, dropping to the mid 40s to around 50 by 9PM. Aside from a few light showers around, conditions should be pleasant with generally light winds. While portions of Carbon and Albany county will be breezy during the daytime hours, expect this to weaken by the evening.

Sunday will be a transition day as a complex storm system approaches from the west. Southwest flow aloft will support the advection of very deep tropical moisture. Precipitable water is expected to surge rapidly through the day Sunday pushing close to climatological maximums by the end of the day. With the aggressive moisture advection, we should see mostly cloudy skies over most of the area, and thus temperatures a few degrees cooler than Saturday. Forcing for ascent will push in Sunday morning in the form of positive theta- e advection and isentropic ascent. This looks most prominent along and west of the Laramie range as it will take a little longer to reach saturation further east. Expect numerous to widespread showers in Carbon County through much of the day, which will gradually push east into at least Albany and Converse counties later in the day. Further east, rainfall will be more spotty, with little to no rain expected in far southeast Wyoming and the central/southern Nebraska panhandle. With falling surface pressure over southwest Wyoming during this period, expect breezy south to southeast winds over much of the area during the day Sunday. Lift is expected to shut off sometime between sunset and midnight Sunday evening as the axis of the first mid-level shortwave trough swings through the area. This will put much of the area in a lull Sunday night into Monday morning.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The approaching storm system continues to look rather messy. Multiple competing upper level lows will make for a muddy forcing picture across the region. A deep primary trough will be making its way across the western CONUS while a moisture laden upper level low riding the sub-tropical jet races in around it. The primary 700-mb low and the secondary center associated with the subtropical system will both pass through the area Sunday evening, leading to drier conditions over much of the area Monday morning. After passing our area, these two should consolidate into one system and stack on top of a rapidly developing surface cyclone. This should take over around daybreak Monday, setting up a strong pressure gradient over the High Plains and leading to increasing northwest winds Monday morning. Widespread gusty northwest winds can be expected Monday into Monday night over the High Plains. Confidence remains high in fairly widespread gusts of 45 to 55 mph, with still some potential to exceed High Wind criteria. Probabilities are generally around 30 to 40% for all along and east of the Laramie range, including the wind prone areas around the I-80 summit and I-25 between Wheatland and Glendo. The wind direction is not very favorable for high winds at Bordeaux. The lack of vertically stacked westerlies and potential for synoptic ascent rather than descent as surface winds increase decreases confidence in widespread high winds.

Forcing will not really favor much lift during this period Monday AM, so expect fairly limited coverage around dawn, but this should change as the day progresses. Model guidance is now in fairly good agreement showing the mid-level low pressure elongating back to the southeast after it passes through our area. This will be forced by lee cyclogenesis ahead of the the primary upper level low swinging over the Four Corners which begins to slow down as it ejects to the east. This appears to be a very complex evolution, but the end result is to turn the wind direction in the 700 to 500-mb layer from northwest Monday morning to north or even northeast by Monday afternoon. Despite surface downslope northwesterly winds continuing, we may see support for ascent just above the surface layer. Where northwest flow is not as unfavorable (Douglas to Chadron corridor), seeing an increase in appreciable rainfall is more promising. The surface downslope will be tough to overcome around the Cheyenne to Sidney corridor. Thus, we appear to be finally converging on the scenario with moderate precipitation in our northern zones, and more limited precipitation further south.

The latest QPF probabilities reflect the increasing confidence in this scenario. LREF probabilities for 0.5" or more of liquid precipitation are around 50 to 60% in Rawlins, Douglas, and Chadron, which look like the most favorable areas at this time, though it is worth mentioning that at least for Rawlins some of this will come from the first phase Sunday and Sunday night, with a break early Monday morning, and then another round Monday late morning into the evening. Precipitation evolution may take on the character of typical northerly flow events across our area, with the subtle terrain features of the High Plains becoming unusually prominent. Specifically, look for more precipitation along the north sides of the Pine Ridge and Cheyenne ridge, with lower totals into the Wheatland to Bridgeport corridor and I-80 corridor (including Cheyenne) and points southward. Laramie and the I-80 summit will be an area to watch for greater uncertainty. This is a pretty unusual synoptic setup with veering winds above surface northwest winds, but that surface direction is favorable for increased precipitation around the city of Laramie.

The last piece of the puzzle with this storm system will be snow levels. Snow levels will be fairly high for most of the event, especially during the first phase where rain may fall as high as 9 to 10 kft. However, we can expect gradual advection of colder air during the day on Monday to reduce snow levels. By sunset, 700-mb temperatures should be below 0C over most of southeast Wyoming. As precipitation picks back up midday Monday into the evening, rain may change over to snow between 5000 ft and 8000 ft. The precise snow level will probably depend on the precipitation rates, with areas of heavier precipitation changing over faster, while lighter rates stay as rain. The problem with this is that there is considerable high end boom scenario potential on snow accumulation if a given area flips over faster than expected. The primary areas to watch right now are Douglas, Lusk, Harrison, and possibly Laramie and the Chugwater area. For now, no snow accumulation is in the official forecast because this is still a low-probability (30% chance) but high impact scenario. However, snow levels were blended to the NBM 10th percentile to ensure the mention of snow is included for these areas of concern.

A much drier airmass will rotate into the area after midnight Monday night, bringing an abrupt end to precipitation from north to south. Gusty northwest winds will continue into Tuesday, but temperatures should rebound to near seasonal averages. The remainder of the week looks to remain somewhat unsettled, with a series of moisture- starved upper level lows pushing across the region. Low-end chances for light precipitation will be present with temperatures near seasonal norms. If some of these lows track slightly to our north, we may have to watch for some gusty winds in the wind prone areas, but most ensemble members keep winds light during this period. By the end of the week into the weekend, we may have another closed low tracking across the west to keep an eye on. Uncertainty is extremely high at this lead-time, but about 1/4 of ensemble members have a closed upper level low tracking over the right area to bring widespread precipitation to the area. However, the remaining 3/4 members are either dry or with minimal precipitation.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: We mentioned 3 or more inches of QPE in the San Juans with this storm system, but much of this water is expected to come down as snow as cold air underneath the passing trough moves overhead.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Showers continue through Friday night. Lower chances of precipitation Saturday afternoon.
- Flooding/flash flooding concerns increase Sunday into Monday, especially for areas that have saturated soils from last week's rain. A Flood Watch remains in effect.
- Winter weather highlights have been issued for the San Juans and central Colorado mountains for accumulating snow Sunday morning through Monday evening.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: RAIN SHOWERS FRIDAY NIGHT AND SATURDAY EVENING:

A band of rainfall driven by a transient shortwave is steadily moving through the region tonight. Impacts will be minimal, though we have seen a stronger embedded thunderstorm or two develop, so don't rule out a few stronger outflow gusts. Otherwise, rainfall is steady and light. Per CAM's, the line of showers will continue northeastwards before departing the CWA late Saturday morning, making way for a relatively calm Saturday afternoon thanks to a "dry" spell. We're using the term "dry" very lightly as PWAT's will still be about 150% of normal (give or take 50% depending on which ensemble you listen to). This is enough to produce a few isolated showers across the region, so don't be surprised if you see a brief bout of rainfall during the afternoon hours. For most of the region though, little more than cloudy skies is to be expected through 6:00 PM MDT. After 6:00 PM, the upper-level jet strengthens overhead, which could produce a few stronger thunderstorms south of US-50 which may bolster a very slight flash flood risk should localized heavily rainfall track over vulnerable areas. As things stand now though, impacts are expected to be minimal and/or very localized.
RAINFALL, SNOWY MOUNTAINS, AND POTENTIAL FLOODING:

A robust Atmospheric River arrives on Sunday bringing well above normal amounts of moisture for this time of year across the Desert Southwest. Guidance continues to show precipitation arriving at the Four Corners region Sunday before sunrise and spreading northeastwards throughout the morning. The ECMWF Ens is running wetter than the GFS Ens for this storm with PWAT's about 0.1-0.25 inches higher in the former regionwide (and as a result, similar margins regarding QPF). So, we do still lack some confidence on the exact magnitude of precipitation accumulations. As far as the NBM is indicating though, areas along the US-160 corridor east of Cortez have a 50-70% of seeing 2 or more inches of rainfall. At higher elevations in the San Juans, QPE is expected to sit over 3 inches in most areas. Considering the notable rainfall these same areas experienced last week, flooding concerns are back on the table, and a Flood Watch is in place. More in the Hydrology section below.

We mentioned 3 or more inches of QPE in the San Juans with this storm system, but much of this water is expected to come down as snow as cold air underneath the passing trough moves overhead. Temperatures will begin to be more noticeably affected beginning near mid-afternoon Sunday as high temperatures are stunted, reaching only into the low-to-mid 50's for valleys and the 30's to low-40's for most mountain locations (with some areas unlikely surpass freezing during the day). Cold air advection will continue throughout the night as well as the storm progresses. What this means for precipitation across the region is that snow levels will begin relatively high Sunday afternoon (around 11,000 feet) before descending over the next 24-36 hours, likely reaching as low as 7,500 to 8,000 feet. Snow ratios wouldn't be overly impressive given the anticipated temperatures, but given the amount of available moisture we'll be experiencing, sufficient factors are in place for well over a foot of snow in the San Juan mountains. Confidence is low on a range of snow accumulations given the transition from rain to snow for most areas, but 14-20 inches currently looks like the most likely range above 11,000 feet and much more variable accumulations below this elevation. In the central Colorado mountains, locations above 11,000 feet are in line for 10-15 inches of snow, meanwhile the Grand Mesa and Flat Tops, considering their lower elevations, are facing 6-12 inches. As a result, Winter Weather highlights are in effect Sunday and Monday. In passes, snow may be slushy given the lower snow ratios, so be mindful should you be traveling through the mountains Sunday or Monday.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Tuesday - Friday: For the remainder of the long term period, periods of active weather are likely for portions of south central and southeastern Colorado.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Showers early for Halloween Day, with mostly dry conditions for the afternoon and evening.
- High impact and dangerous flooding likely early next week as another strong storm system bring heavy precipitation to the southwestern Mountains.
- An unsettled pattern continues next week after Monday for the region.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Today and Tonight: Happy Halloween!!!! For the spooky day, nothing too scary going on weather wise for south central and southeastern Colorado. Overall, broad southwesterly flow will be in place throughout the day, bringing only modest moisture and forcing. An embedded shortwave will drift over early in the day however, which will bring a brief boost to forcing. With this uptick in ascent, scattered showers are expected early in the day across mostly the mountains and valleys, where orographic forcing will better support precipitation. Light snow can be expected along the mountains, generally from 10,000-10,300+ft, with rain below that. While snow will be relatively light, slick spots on roads can't be ruled out, so extra caution should be given along mountain road ways early. With that all said, subsidence will increase behind the wave as it exits early, with dry conditions then prevailing through the day and into the overnight hours. A rouge shower or two can't be ruled out across the higher terrain where terrain influences may still help a shower blossom. Beyond all of that, winds will remain fairly light, around and less than 10 mph, with mostly cloudy skies early giving way to partly skies during the afternoon, before clouds start to increase in coverage again during the evening hours. As for temperatures, both highs and lows will be above seasonal values for late October. Highs for the plains will be in the low 60s to low 70s, for the valleys in the upper 40s to 50s, and for the mountains in the low 30s to upper 40s. For the lows, the plains will be in the upper 30s to 40, for the valleys in the 30s to low 40s, and for the mountains in the mid 20s to 30s.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Sunday and Monday: For the start of November, an active couple of days is anticipated, with high impact flooding expected across the already soaked southwestern mountains. A dynamic storm pattern will take shape, with the sub-tropical jet pushing northward, and a digging trough interacting with this. Confidence at this point is very high (>80%) in this upcoming pattern. As these two large scale features interact, another round of prolonged and heavy precipitation is anticipated across our mountains, with the heaviest falling across the San Juan Mountains. On the front side of this storm system, the airmass will be relatively warm, leading to higher snow levels Sunday, around 11,000-12,000+ft, and rain for a majority of the region. Then on the backside of the system, cooler Pacific air will filter in and drop snow levels to around 9,000-10,000ft by Monday morning. Overall, the warm and moist nature of this storm system is what will cause issues. This will favor a significant amount of precipitation falling as rain, with QPF totals ranging from 2-4 inches. This amount of liquid on top of already highly saturated soils, water laden snow, and running into rivers that are already elevated from last weeks rain event, will likely lead to another highly impactful flood event across the southwestern mountains and into the San Luis Valley. Currently, local rivers in that region are forecasted to quickly rise into Moderate to Major flood stages heading through Monday, with some rivers nearing record crest levels. Folks, the window for flood preparations is closing. Preparations should be ongoing and finished by this afternoon. Do not wait until it starts to rain and do not wait until the waters start to rise... by then it is too late. Then as alluded to, snow levels will start to lower heading through Sunday night and into Monday morning, which will transition some of the rain into snow, with around 12-15 inches of heavy, wet snow anticipated with this entire storm system. This will likely cause travel impacts along the southwestern mountain roadways, with dangerous and slick road conditions, especially Sunday night into Monday morning. Across the rest of the higher terrain, additional heavy, wet snow can be expected, though to a lesser degree, with ranges typically from 4-10 inches. Elsewhere for the valleys and plains, rain scattered to numerous showers can be expected through this period. The greatest coverage for the valleys will be Sunday, with the greatest coverage then shifting eastward across the plains Monday as the storm system pushes east and a cold front drops southward. Along with all of that, strong winds can be expected both days, with gusty southwesterly winds Sunday on the front side of the storm system, with gusts of 30-50 mph, especially for the mountains, San Luis Valley, and eastern plains. Then gusty winds can be expected again Monday, as northwesterly winds develop on the backside of the storm system, with gusts again 30-50 mph, especially across the eastern plains. There is potential for winds to be stronger across the plains Monday night into Tuesday morning, but confidence on that is low (30%) at this time, at it will be highly dependent on how the trough evolves Monday night. Finally, to round things out for this stretch, mostly cloudy to cloudy skies can be anticipated with the stormy pattern in place, with temperatures warm and above seasonal values Sunday, and then cooling some Monday as the system passes and the aforementioned cold front starts dropping southward.

Tuesday - Friday: For the remainder of the long term period, periods of active weather are likely for portions of south central and southeastern Colorado. Overall, an active pattern will continue, with the Sunday - Monday storm system exiting Tuesday and additional waves within the flow passing over the region after that. Tuesday's exiting system will bring gusty winds early in the day, especially across the plains, with the later week features bringing increased precipitation chances, particularly for the mountains. While uncertainty does exist in how some of these waves will ultimately evolve, confidence is high (60-70%) about the unsettled pattern. Otherwise, breezy winds and uptick in cloud cover can be anticipated with these wave passages. As for temperatures, a fairly steady trend of mild temperatures can be expected.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: The trough is expected to exit the area Monday morning, with just a few mountain showers expected to linger into Monday afternoon. Temperatures will be quite unseasonably cool, with maxes averaging 10-15F below seasonal normals.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - After a relative lull in precipitation on Saturday, an atmospheric river will interact with a strong cold front Sunday into Monday, resulting in widespread moderate to heavy precipitation across the region. This will increase the potential for flash flooding on Sunday across southern and eastern Utah.

- Accumulating mountain snow is expected Sunday night through early Monday as colder air spreads into the region. Local snowfall totals above 8000 feet may exceed 12" across areas favored in northwest flow.
- Cool, dry and stable conditions are expected Tuesday into Wednesday, before a more active pattern returns later next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Utah and southwest Wyoming remain under a south to southwest flow this evening which has brought unseasonably high moisture to much of the area, particularly over southern Utah. Satellite derived PWs are in the 0.6 to 0.8 inch range over southern Utah and 0.3 to 0.5 inch elsewhere. This allowed for good coverage of showers today, particularly along a line extending from southwest Utah through the Wasatch Front where some embedded shortwave energy moved through.

The remaining shortwave energy with exit to the north tonight, taking some of the moisture with it. This will result in a relative lull in precipitation on Saturday with just some scattered showers around. High temperatures are expected to stay near seasonal normals across northern portions of the area, but in excess of 5F below climo over southern Utah where more cloud cover is expected.

Confidence remains high that ingredients will come together to bring widespread valley rain and mountain snow to Utah and southwest Wyoming Sunday into Monday. Southerly flow will bring up moisture from a landfalling atmospheric river as a strong and progressive Pacific storm system tracks across the state. With this high amount of moisture and instability, rain will be heavy at times, creating a rather heightened potential for flash flooding, particularly for southern Utah. Going Flood Watch covers this threat well.

As the strong cold front moves through, snow levels are expected to lower from 9,000 feet to as low as the 6,500 to 7,000 foot range, bringing accumulating snow to all of Utah's mountains. These totals could be significant, particularly for areas favored in northwest flow, and this has the potential to bring travel difficulties to higher elevation routes.

The trough is expected to exit the area Monday morning, with just a few mountain showers expected to linger into Monday afternoon. Temperatures will be quite unseasonably cool, with maxes averaging 10-15F below seasonal normals. Weak transient high pressure is then expected to keep conditions dry for Tuesday, but most guidance shows this being quickly pushed out of the way by yet another Pacific trough Wednesday into Thursday, with an active pattern then continuing through at least day seven. Ensemble spread remains high with regard to the timing, strength, and track of these individual systems so confidence is low with regard to potential impacts, but relatively high in the continued unsettled pattern.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: An avalanche accident on the east side of Mt. Bross highlights that you can trigger a dangerous avalanche at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) of the Central and Southern Mountains. West, north, and east-facing slopes hold multiple layers of snow from several storms in October. Deeper, wind-drifted slopes may be the most enticing for early-season snow travel, but they're also the slopes most likely to release an avalanche one to two feet deep.

Clouds build from the southwest on Friday ahead of a small initial wave of moisture. Friday night, expect light rain below around 10,000 feet, and up to six or eight inches of snow in the favored portions of the San Juan Mountains by Saturday morning, with less precipitation to the north. Saturday, the moisture tap dries out, before a stronger storm rolls in early Sunday.

On Sunday, a deep east-bound low-pressure trough brings initially warm conditions, with snow levels around 11,000 feet. Sunday night into early Monday, a cold front intensifies snowfall and pushes snow levels down to around 8,000 feet. By the end of the day Monday, expect storm totals of 1 to 2 feet of snow in the San Juan Mountains with half that amount through the Central and Northern Mountains.
Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
